text: Patent infringement occurs when someone makes, uses, sells, offers for sale, or imports a patented invention without authorization. Section 48 defines patentee's exclusive rights. Types: Direct infringement (actual unauthorized use), Indirect/contributory infringement (supplying components knowing they'll be used to infringe), Inducement (actively encouraging others to infringe). For AYUSH patents: infringement typically involves manufacturing or selling a formulation that falls within claim scope. Compare accused product with claim elements — all elements must be present for literal infringement.

In infringement analysis, claims are construed (interpreted) to determine their scope. Principles: 1) Claims interpreted in light of specification. 2) Each claim term given its ordinary meaning unless specifically defined. 3) Prosecution history (file wrapper) can limit claim scope. 4) Claims are not expanded to cover subject matter not claimed. For AYUSH: if claim says '5-10% Ashwagandha extract', accused product with 12% may not literally infringe. Consider doctrine of equivalents for minor variations.

Even if no literal infringement, infringement may occur under doctrine of equivalents if accused product performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result (function-way-result test). Limits: cannot recapture subject matter surrendered during prosecution, must still have equivalent element for each claim element. For AYUSH: if claim says 'aqueous extract' and accused uses 'hydroalcoholic extract' achieving same effect, may be equivalent. Case-by-case analysis required.

Remedies for patent infringement under Section 108: 1) Injunction — court order to stop infringing activity (interim and permanent). 2) Damages — compensation for losses suffered. 3) Account of profits — surrender of infringer's profits from infringement. 4) Seizure/destruction of infringing goods. 5) Costs — legal fees recovery. Plaintiff chooses damages OR account of profits (not both). For AYUSH: injunction stopping competitor's product is often most valuable remedy; damages calculation complex for pharmaceutical market.

Interim (temporary) injunction can stop alleged infringement during litigation. Requirements (from tripartite test): 1) Prima facie case of infringement. 2) Balance of convenience favors plaintiff. 3) Irreparable injury if injunction not granted. Courts also consider: public interest, plaintiff's delay in filing, relative harm to parties. For AYUSH: interim injunction can remove competitor's product from market during case, but courts hesitant if essential medicine and public health impact.

Patent infringement suit filed in District Court (post-2016 amendment) or High Court (commercial division for higher value). Process: 1) File plaint with claim chart showing infringement. 2) Ex parte application for interim injunction if urgent. 3) Defendant files written statement, possibly counterclaim for revocation. 4) Discovery/document production. 5) Expert evidence if technical issues. 6) Trial and arguments. 7) Judgment. Timeline: 1-5 years typically. High Courts in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai handle most IP cases.

In infringement suits, defendant can counterclaim for patent revocation on any ground under Section 64: 1) Wrongful obtaining. 2) Prior publication. 3) Prior claiming. 4) Prior use/public knowledge. 5) Obviousness. 6) Non-patentable subject matter (Section 3). 7) Insufficient disclosure. 8) Non-compliance with Section 8 (foreign filing info). For AYUSH: defendants often challenge validity under Section 3(d) (no enhanced efficacy), 3(p) (traditional knowledge), or 3(e) (mere admixture). Strong patent prosecution reduces revocation risk.

IPR holders can record patents, trademarks, copyrights with Customs to stop infringing imports. Intellectual Property Rights (Imported Goods) Enforcement Rules 2007 govern the process. Procedure: 1) Apply to Customs Commissioner with IP details, expected importers, identifying features. 2) If recorded, Customs can detain suspected infringing goods at ports. 3) IP holder inspects and confirms infringement. 4) Goods seized/destroyed if confirmed infringing. For AYUSH: useful to stop import of counterfeit or infringing formulations, especially from countries with manufacturing capacity.

Trademark counterfeiting in AYUSH sector is rampant — fake Ayurvedic products with copied brands. Criminal provisions: Section 103-104 of Trade Marks Act — imprisonment up to 3 years, fine up to Rs 2 lakh for using false trademarks. Civil remedies: injunction, damages, destruction of goods. Enforcement options: 1) Police complaint (cognizable offense). 2) Civil suit in District/High Court. 3) Customs recordal for imports. 4) Market surveys and raids through enforcement agencies. For AYUSH: protect brands aggressively; counterfeits harm reputation and may pose health risks.

Protect AYUSH products from counterfeiting: 1) Trademark registration (obvious but essential). 2) Holographic labels — difficult to replicate. 3) QR codes linking to authentication system. 4) Unique packaging design (register as design). 5) Serial number tracking. 6) Customer awareness campaigns — how to identify genuine products. 7) Market monitoring — online and offline. 8) Swift enforcement action against detected counterfeits. 9) Work with industry associations and regulatory bodies. Investment in anti-counterfeiting pays off in brand protection and consumer safety.

IP disputes can be resolved through ADR: 1) Mediation — neutral mediator facilitates negotiation, non-binding. 2) Arbitration — binding decision by arbitrator(s), faster than courts. 3) Expert determination — for technical valuation issues. Advantages: faster, cheaper, confidential, preserved business relationships. Commercial Courts Act mandates pre-institution mediation for many cases. For AYUSH: license negotiations, joint venture disputes, distributor conflicts often better resolved through mediation than litigation.

IP rights can interface with competition law. Competition Act 2002 Section 3(5) exempts reasonable IP conditions from anti-competitive agreements prohibition. But abuse of dominant position through IP (excessive pricing, refusal to license) can violate Section 4. Compulsory licensing provisions in Patents Act reflect competition concerns. For AYUSH patent holders: exercise rights reasonably; don't create market foreclosure or abuse dominance. License terms should be commercially reasonable.

Enforcing AYUSH IP internationally: 1) Register IP in each target country. 2) Use Madrid Protocol for trademarks, PCT national phases for patents. 3) Monitor for infringement through watch services. 4) Work with local counsel for enforcement. 5) Customs recordal in key markets. 6) Consider international arbitration for contract disputes. Challenges: different laws, expensive multi-jurisdiction litigation, enforcement difficulties in some countries. Focus on key markets and build local relationships.

Section 106 provides remedy against groundless threats of patent infringement. If patent holder threatens without basis (patent invalid, no actual infringement), threatened party can sue for: 1) Declaration that threats are unjustifiable. 2) Injunction against continuation of threats. 3) Damages for losses from threats. Exception: mere notification of patent existence is not a threat. For AYUSH: before sending cease-and-desist letters, ensure solid infringement analysis. Empty threats can backfire legally and reputationally.

Building infringement case requires evidence: 1) Purchase accused products — trap purchase with witnesses. 2) Laboratory analysis — compare composition with claims. 3) Expert opinion — technical infringement analysis. 4) Market evidence — sales data, advertisements. 5) Prior art search — if expecting validity challenge. 6) Prosecution history — for claim interpretation. Indian courts allow: Anton Piller orders (search and seizure), John Doe orders (against unknown infringers), discovery during trial. For AYUSH: retain samples, document everything, use accredited labs for analysis.
